title: Conditional Types and infer
summary: Choose between two types with a condition, see how conditions spread over unions, and pull types out of promises, arrays, and functions with infer.
intro: Some types depend on other types. A `Date` in your code is a string once it's JSON, and a handler's payload is whatever its parameter says. Conditional types write such rules down: if this type fits that one, use one type, else another. They're how `Exclude`, `Extract`, `ReturnType`, and `Awaited` are written, and how library types adapt to what you pass them. In this lesson you write your own, see how they behave on unions, and use `infer` to take one type out of another.

steps.title: Conditional types

examples.title: Naming a type
examples.prompt: Name the type of a value with a chain of conditions, and make a function's second argument depend on its first.

examples.title: NonNullable from scratch
examples.prompt: Write your own NonNullable with a condition, and compare it with the built-in.
examples.output:
Hello, Ada!
Hello, guest!
Hello, Grace!
Hello, guest!
examples.explanation: A member that fits `null | undefined` becomes `never`, and every other member stays as it is, so only `string` is left. That works because a condition on a type parameter checks a union one member at a time, which the next part explains. `never` is the empty type, so it disappears from any union. The built-in gets the same answer another way: the library declares `NonNullable<T>` as `T & {}`, and `{}` accepts every value except `null` and `undefined`. In the loop, the check narrows `n` to `string`, which is exactly `Name`.

examples.title: An item or a list of items
examples.prompt: Get the type of one item from config fields that hold either a single value or a list.
examples.explanation: For an array, `T[number]` is the type of its items, the same `[number]` indexing that turns an `as const` array into the union of its items. Anything that isn't an array comes back as it is, so `Port` is just `number`. The check uses `readonly unknown[]` on purpose: a normal array fits a readonly one, but not the other way round. With `unknown[]`, the readonly `sizes` tuple would fail the check and come back whole, instead of as the union of its three sizes.

practice.title: JSON shapes
practice.prompt:
Describe what an order looks like once it's JSON, where every `Date` is a string, and convert an order to that shape.

1. Make `ApiField<T>` a conditional type: `string` when `T` is a `Date`, else `T` itself.
2. Make `Jsonified<T>` a mapped type that gives each key `K` of `T` the type `ApiField<T[K]>`.
3. Make `toJson` return the order with `createdAt` turned into a string with `toISOString()`, with the keys in the order `id`, `createdAt`, `totalCents`. A `Date` in a template string prints its long local form, so the first line shows whether `createdAt` really became a string.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `ApiField`, `Jsonified`, `Order`, and `toJson`.

Expected output:

```text
Placed at 2026-10-01T09:00:00.000Z
{"id":"ord_1001","createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00.000Z","totalCents":4599}
```

typeTests.imports: import { toJson, type ApiField, type Jsonified, type Order } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: toJson returns the JSON shape of an order
cases.code:
declare const o: Order;
const j: Jsonified<Order> = toJson(o);

cases.name: createdAt is no longer a Date
cases.code:
declare const j: Jsonified<Order>;
const d: Date = j.createdAt;

cases.name: createdAt is a string
cases.code:
declare const j: Jsonified<Order>;
const s: string = j.createdAt;

cases.name: keeps the fields that aren't dates
cases.code:
declare const j: Jsonified<Order>;
const n: number = j.totalCents;

cases.name: turns a Date into a string

hints: `TypeName` in the first example chains two conditions. `ApiField` needs only one: `T extends Date ? ... : ...`.
`Jsonified` maps over the keys like the types in the Mapped Types lesson, with `ApiField<T[K]>` after the colon.
`return { id: order.id, createdAt: order.createdAt.toISOString(), totalCents: order.totalCents };`

steps.title: Distribution over unions

examples.title: One list type per member
examples.prompt: Type a column of a table, which holds only strings or only numbers, never both.

examples.title: Exclude from scratch
examples.prompt: Write Exclude yourself, and follow how it removes members from a union.
examples.output:
Mapped types: Live
Conditional types: In review
examples.explanation: `MyExclude` checks each member of `Status` on its own. `"draft"` fits `"draft" | "archived"`, so it becomes `never`. `"review"` doesn't, so it stays, and so does `"published"`. `"archived"` becomes `never`. The four results make the union `never | "review" | "published" | never`, and the two `never`s drop out. The library declares `Exclude` with this exact line, which is why the bubbles match. `BADGES` is a `Record<Live, string>`, so it needs a badge for both live statuses, and a badge for `"draft"` would be an error.

examples.title: Turning distribution off
examples.prompt: Type a row of a table, which mixes strings and numbers, by checking the union as a whole.
examples.explanation: In `ToMixedArray`, the condition checks `[T]`, a one-item tuple, instead of `T` itself, so it doesn't distribute. `T` stays the whole union, and `Row` is one array type whose items may be strings or numbers, as the bubble shows. A table needs both types: a column holds one kind of value, and a row mixes them. The brackets are the usual way to turn distribution off, and you'll meet them in library types wherever a union must be treated as one type.

practice.title: Events with a user
practice.prompt:
Keep only the events that carry a user id, both in the types and in the data, and list the users who show up.

1. Make `HasField<T, K>` a conditional type that keeps `T` when it fits `Record<K, unknown>`, which means it has a field named `K`, and gives `never` otherwise. On a union, it keeps just the members with that field.
2. Make `hasUser` return `true` for the events that have a `userId`.
3. After the count, print `Users:` followed by the user ids in the order they first appear, without repeats, separated by a comma and a space.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `AppEvent`, `HasField`, `WithUser`, and `hasUser`.

Expected output:

```text
5 of 7 events have a user
Users: u1, u2, u3
```

tests.output:
5 of 7 events have a user
Users: u1, u2, u3

typeTests.imports: import { hasUser, type AppEvent, type HasField, type WithUser } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: works on any union
cases.code: const n: HasField<{ name: string } | { id: number }, "name"> = { name: "Ada" };

cases.name: drops the members without the field
cases.code: const n: HasField<{ name: string } | { id: number }, "name"> = { id: 1 };

cases.name: narrows an event to one with a user

hints: A member fits `Record<K, unknown>` when it has a field named `K`, whatever that field holds. Keep it with `T` and drop it with `never`, the way `MyExclude` in the second example drops members.
`"userId" in e` is `true` for exactly the events with a user. A `Set` keeps the first of each value in the order it was added.
`export type HasField<T, K extends string> = T extends Record<K, unknown> ? T : never;` and `new Set(withUser.map((e) => e.userId))`

steps.title: Pulling types out with infer

examples.title: Unwrapping a promise
examples.prompt: Unwrap the value of a promise with infer, and compare your version with the built-in Awaited.
examples.explanation: `ReturnType<typeof loadUser>` is a promise of a user, and `Unwrap` takes the user out of it, the same type `await` gives you. `Unwrap` looks only one level deep, so a promise of a promise leaves a promise behind. `Awaited` unwraps every level, as `await` itself does. Use `Awaited` in real code. Writing `Unwrap` shows how it works inside.

examples.title: The item type of an array
examples.prompt: Get the item type of any array with infer, and use it for a list of sizes kept as data.
examples.explanation: `readonly (infer E)[]` matches any array, readonly or not, and names the type of its items `E`. The parentheses around `infer E` are required: without them, `tsc` can't parse the line. On the `SIZES` tuple, `E` is the union of the four sizes, so `PRICES` must price every size. A `string` isn't an array, so it gets `never`, which tells you the type was used on the wrong thing. When you have the array itself, `(typeof SIZES)[number]` gives the same union. `infer` earns its place when the array sits inside something else, as in `T extends { items: readonly (infer E)[] } ? E : never` for the items of a page of results.

examples.title: A function's first parameter
examples.prompt: Name the type of a function's first parameter with infer, and build the arguments for it ahead of time.
examples.output:
welcome-v2 to Ada <ada@example.com>
welcome-v2 to Grace <grace@example.com>
examples.explanation: The pattern is a function type with `infer A` as its first parameter, so `A` becomes whatever `sendWelcome` takes first: here an inline user type that had no name of its own. `...rest: never[]` lets the pattern match a function with any number of further parameters, because `never` fits every parameter type. The return type is `unknown` because any return type will do. `Parameters<typeof sendWelcome>[0]` gives the same type, and `FirstArg` shows how such a type is built.

practice.title: Handler payloads
practice.prompt:
Infer each handler's payload type, then line up payloads for both handlers and run them.

1. Make `PayloadOf<F>` a conditional type that matches `F` against a function with one parameter, `(payload: infer P) => void`, and gives `P`, or `never` when `F` doesn't match.
2. Type `greetings` as a list of `handlers.greet` payloads and `sums` as a list of `handlers.add` payloads, with `PayloadOf` and `typeof`.
3. Call `handlers.greet` on each greeting, then `handlers.add` on each sum, and print each result.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `handlers` and `PayloadOf`.

Expected output:

```text
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Grace!
2 + 3 = 5
10 + -4 = 6
```

cases.name: a greet payload has a name
an add payload needs both numbers
a name must be a string
is never for something that isn't a function

hints: `FirstArg` in the third example matches the first of several parameters. A handler has just one, so its pattern is simpler: `(payload: infer P) => void`.
`typeof handlers.greet` is the type of the greet function, so `PayloadOf<typeof handlers.greet>[]` is a list of its payloads.
`export type PayloadOf<F> = F extends (payload: infer P) => void ? P : never;`

recap:
- `T extends U ? X : Y` is `X` when `T` fits `U`, else `Y`. Chain conditions like ternaries to test several cases.
- On a bare type parameter, a condition distributes: a union is checked one member at a time, and members that become `never` drop out. `Exclude` and `Extract` work this way.
- `[T] extends [U]` checks a union as a whole, with no distribution.
- `infer X` in the `extends` part names a piece of the matched type for the true branch. `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, and `Awaited` are built with it.
- Conditional types exist only for `tsc`. To check a value while the program runs, use `typeof`, `in`, and type guards.
